contract_plain_english: The physical conservation law says that an interval's total conserved quantity changes through the difference of its endpoint fluxes, and the text retains integral conservation for discontinuous solutions (printed pp. 4–5, (1.10) and Section 1.1.2). Finite volume methods use cell integrals or cell averages, with each average defined by division by cell volume, and update these quantities through cell-edge fluxes (printed p. 5, Section 1.2). Given neighboring cell averages Q_{i−1} and Q_i, they are used as the left and right constant states of a Riemann problem. Solving that problem provides information usable to compute a numerical flux and update cell averages over a time step (printed p. 5, (1.11) and following paragraph). The passage specifies neither the information object nor a flux formula, update formula, quantitative accuracy bound, or general solvability theorem; the surrounding discussion also allows approximate Riemann solvers (printed pp. 5–6, Section 1.2.1).
